rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. The midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to probe selectivity of the single critical pair at R 0.82. All peaks already elute within 10 minutes, so resolving that pair without compromising neighboring pairs could reach the maximum score.

The central peak pattern suggests a temperature-driven order reversal, so increasing to 55 C may separate the critical pair further. A slightly shallower gradient should protect the neighboring pair that narrowed at 50 C while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Keep the favorable 55 C selectivity and make the gradient one step shallower to lift the critical pair from R 1.47 above 1.5. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, allowing a maximum CRF if all pairs resolve.

The shallower gradient reduced critical-pair resolution, so shorten the gradient to 12 minutes at the same temperature. Extrapolating the observed trend suggests R may exceed 1.5 while the neighboring pair remains resolved and the last peak elutes earlier.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient one step to test whether full resolution can be retained with an earlier last peak. Watch the pair at R 1.59, which narrowed as the gradient became steeper, and retain injection 5 as the proven best method.

Shortening to 10 minutes compromised resolution, so restore the successful 12-minute duration and raise the starting organic fraction one step. This tests whether a narrower gradient window can advance the last peak while preserving full resolution; injection 5 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover the pair that fell to R 1.29 after raising the starting organic fraction. This may retain the narrower window’s time advantage while restoring full resolution; injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a cooler selectivity regime for the shorter gradient. The temperature-driven central peak reordering suggests cooling could open a different resolution window, while the broad gradient limits the risk of late or missing peaks.

Test a faster, high-temperature selectivity regime to see whether the narrowing central pair separates again after an elution-order reversal. This is exploratory; injection 5 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

The peak-width pattern suggests the critical pair has reversed order at 60 C; a steeper gradient may now widen its separation. Test one shorter step while monitoring neighboring pairs, retaining injection 5 as the proven maximum-score method.

Return to the near-resolved window from injection 8 and lower phi1 one step to improve its R 1.47 pair. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes and may provide a second maximum-score method with better minimum-resolution margin than injection 5.

Shift and narrow the successful window from injection 12 to test whether both critical pairs gain resolution margin while the last peak stays below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this explores a potentially more robust maximum-score alternative.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction separates the reversed central pair in the fast 60 C regime without the neighboring-pair collapse seen at six minutes. Injection 5 remains the proven maximum-score method while this explores a substantially faster alternative.

Raise the starting organic fraction to further separate the reversed critical pair, while lengthening the gradient to protect its neighboring pair at R 1.62. Monitor the early peaks for compression; injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Test an intermediate-temperature selectivity window with a short gradient, since 25 C produced extensive crowding and the fast 60 C methods retained a critical overlap. Keep the low starting organic fraction to protect early separation, with injection 5 retained as the proven maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 5’s successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute but end the ramp earlier. Because its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this ramp ends at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, this should preserve full resolution and maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Refine injection 13 by lowering the endpoint one step to improve its only unresolved pair, at R 1.41. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially yielding a maximum-score method with more resolution margin than injection 5.

Lower the endpoint one more step from injection 18 to balance its two limiting resolutions and test for a larger minimum-resolution margin. The last peak is projected near 9.8 minutes, so this may retain maximum CRF; injection 5 remains the faster proven method.

Use a slope between injections 8 and 12 to target full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 12. The observed trends suggest the two limiting pairs should both remain above R 1.5, while injection 5 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Keep the proven 0.075-per-minute slope through all closely spaced peaks, then hold at 0.50 organic to test a shorter ramp and lower endpoint. The isolated last peak may elute later, so this tests whether maximum CRF is retained below 10 minutes rather than assuming a shorter ramp means a faster separation.

Test a modestly steeper slope of 0.080 per minute, between the fully resolved method and the unsuccessful 10-minute broad gradient. This probes whether the last peak can elute sooner than 7.60 minutes while retaining full resolution; injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Refine around the fully resolved injection 12 with a slightly shallower gradient, targeting more margin for its R 1.67 pair while monitoring the R 1.58 pair. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes; injection 5 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Back off from injection 22’s excessive slope to the proven 0.075-per-minute slope, using a new endpoint-duration combination. This should reproduce the fastest fully resolved separation at about 7.60 minutes and retain maximum CRF.
